On The Art of Collecting Light

There is a shelf in my mind that doesn't exist anywhere in the physical world. On it sits a collection of things that were never meant to be collected.

A chipped mug from a kitchen I only visited once. The way the air smelled at 5:47 AM on a Tuesday in October when I was nine years old and had woken up too early, and the house was completely silent except for the refrigerator humming. The precise blue of a friend's jacket as he turned to wave goodbye at an airport, knowing we wouldn't see each other for years. A sentence someone said in passing that I have carried for a decade even though they have almost certainly forgotten it.

We talk a lot about memories as if they are videos we file away, but that has never felt quite right to me. They are not videos. They are impressions pressed into soft wax. They are smells and temperatures and fragments of light. And the strange thing is that the most important collection we will ever build is not intentional at all. We don't choose what stays. The shelf fills itself.

I think about this a lot — the involuntary curation of a life.

When I was younger, I believed that a good life was a loud life. That meaning had to be large to count. You had to build something enormous, love someone dramatically, travel far, suffer visibly, succeed unmistakably. I thought significance announced itself with trumpets. I have grown older and quieter, and I now suspect the opposite is true.

Significance whispers.

It lives in the small repetitions that you don't notice until they are gone. The way someone always taps the doorframe twice when they leave a room. The particular way your street looks when it has just rained and the sun comes out and everything is suddenly glossy and new. The sound of a grocery store closing, the carts being lined up, the metal shutters rattling down.

I used to walk through my days half-asleep, waiting for the important part to begin. I was always in the hallway, waiting for the door to open. I told myself: when I finish school, then life will start. When I get that job, then I will be real. When I find that person, then I will be known. It was always a future condition, a contingency plan for existence. I was living in the footnotes, waiting for the main text.

And then, without any ceremony at all, I realized I had been living the main text the entire time.

There was no doorway. The hallway *was* the house.

This realization didn't arrive as a dramatic epiphany. It arrived the way most true things do — slowly, and then all at once, and then slowly again. I was washing dishes. That's all. The water was warm, the light was coming in from the window at that late afternoon angle that makes dust visible, and I had a song stuck in my head that I didn't even particularly like. And I felt, with a sudden and embarrassing clarity, grateful. Not for anything big. Just for the warm water and the light and the fact that I had hands at all.

It sounds small because it is small. That is the whole point.

We have been sold the idea that attention is a limited resource, and that we should spend it only on what is urgent, spectacular, or profitable. The entire economy of our phones is built on stealing that attention and selling it back to us in smaller, more anxious pieces. So we learn to look only at what shouts. We forget how to look at what glows.

But there is a different kind of attention. An older kind. The kind you use when you watch an ant carry a crumb that is three times its size across a sidewalk crack. Or when you watch clouds and see them not as weather, but as sculpture. Or when you listen to a person not to reply, but to understand the shape of their loneliness.

That kind of attention is a form of love. And love, in its purest form, is just sustained attention.

I wonder what would happen if we trained ourselves again to notice. Not to document. Not to photograph. Not to post. Just to notice. To practice what the poet Mary Oliver called “paying attention” — which she said was her real work, and the beginning of devotion.

Attention changes what it falls upon. Have you noticed this? If you stare at an ordinary object long enough — a spoon, a leaf, a crack in the ceiling — it stops being ordinary. It becomes strange, specific, unrepeatable. Every leaf has a map of veins that has never existed before and will never exist again. Every crack is a tiny lightning strike frozen in plaster. The world is not made of generic objects. It is made of 400 billion particulars, each insisting on its own existence.

We skim. The world begs us to linger.

A few years ago I started a practice that felt silly at first. Every night, before I went to sleep, I would try to remember one small, perfect thing from the day that I would have otherwise forgotten. Not the big events. The small ones.

The way the cashier had to push her glasses up her nose because her hands were full. The shadow my coffee cup left on the table that looked exactly like an island. The kid on the bus who fell asleep with his mouth open and his mother kept gently brushing his hair off his forehead so it wouldn't tickle him.

I wrote them down in a cheap notebook. After a few months, I had a hundred of them. After a year, I had more than three hundred tiny lights. And something shifted in my days. Knowing I would be looking for one later made me look for one now. The days became less blurry. They developed texture.

I began to understand that joy is not the opposite of sorrow. It is the companion. They live in the same house. The people who have taught me the most about joy are not the people who have had easy lives, but the people who have learned to hold both at once. Who can say, “This is hard, and this is also beautiful.”

There is a Japanese concept called *mono no aware* — often translated as “the pathos of things” or “an empathy toward things.” It is the bittersweet awareness of impermanence. Cherry blossoms are beautiful not despite the fact that they fall in two weeks, but *because* they fall in two weeks. Their beauty and their briefness are the same thing.

I think we feel this without having words for it. Why else would we be so moved by sunsets? A sunset does nothing. It provides no practical value. It is just light leaving. And yet we stop our cars to watch it. We call other people outside to see it. We know, in some wordless place in our chest, that we are watching time itself become visible.

We are all, whether we want to be or not, collectors of light. The light is always leaving. Our job is to have been there while it was there.

So if I could leave anything here, in these thousand words that you asked me to write freely, it would not be advice. I distrust advice. It would be a permission slip. A small, perhaps unnecessary reminder:

You are allowed to have a quiet life and still have it be meaningful. You are allowed to love small things fiercely. You are allowed to measure your life not by what you have accomplished, but by how tenderly you have noticed.

The world will tell you to hurry. To optimize. To scale. To become more.

But somewhere, in a kitchen at 5:47 AM, a refrigerator is humming. Somewhere, light is falling across a table at the perfect angle. Somewhere, someone is tapping a doorframe twice without even knowing they do it.

And if you happen to be there to see it — truly see it — for a second, you get to keep it forever on that invisible shelf.

That is enough. It has always been enough.

You have already, without trying, built a museum of moments that no one else will ever have. That is your life. That is your work of art. Not what you will do someday, but what you have already, gently, without applause, been doing all along: paying attention to the light as it passes through.
